name: Bianca Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time after school. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach Year 4 at Hollins Road Primary, so thirty-one eight- and nine-year-olds, and this is my second year. I'm in by half seven to set up, then it's maths, phonics catch-up, reading, and after lunch topic work, which this term is the Romans. I share a teaching assistant, Mrs Okafor, with the class next door, so she's with me in the mornings only. The bit I love is when a kid who's been stuck on fractions for a week suddenly gets it and looks at me like I've done magic.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The planning and the data. Every half term we enter reading and maths levels into a tracking system, write comments, and then there's a meeting about the kids who are behind. I'm still slow at it, honestly, so a lot of evenings at the kitchen table go on that. My partner Kwame is a nurse on shifts, so some weeks we barely see each other awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, well, there you go, all that fuss for a slightly better spellchecker. In the staffroom I'd joke that the robots aren't coming for Year 4 because they couldn't survive wet play. Online I'd stay quiet; I don't post much about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my worries in that world are the ones I already have. Our school lost a teaching assistant post last year and the head said budgets are tight again, so I worry about doing more with less help. Rent on our flat went up eighty a month in the summer, and on a second-year salary that bites. AI isn't what keeps me up; the budget is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and get better at it, because I'm still learning the job. I'd use the planning tool the trust gives us now and then for worksheets, maybe an hour saved a week. I'd keep putting a hundred a month into savings and stay in the union, and go to the meeting about the budget in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly normal, a bit tired. It's a relief that nothing big changes, but it's not like normal is easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the budget meeting. What would you actually say there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this: If they cut the teaching assistant's hours again, three kids in my class who need help with reading will just fall further behind. Mrs Okafor is the only reason those three are keeping up. I'm not brave in meetings yet, but our union rep, Daniel, is, so I'd back him up and give him the names and numbers. That's the kind of thing I'm good at, the details of each child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And money at home, what's the plan there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got about three months of bills saved, which feels okay but not great. If rent goes up again next summer, the first thing to go is the gym membership I barely use, and then takeaways on Fridays. A tight school budget means no pay jump beyond the normal step, so I just plan around that.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be a **better spellchecker**, not a revolution.
I'd joke that **wet play** would beat any robot sent into Year 4.
think: My real worries are the **school budget** and losing classroom help.
Our **rent rise** of eighty a month matters more to me than AI does.
do: Use the trust's **planning tool** now and then and save about an hour a week.
Back the union rep at the **January budget meeting** with names and reading data.
Keep putting **£100 a month** into savings and cut the gym if rent rises.
feel: **Relieved** that nothing big changes, but still **tired** by the normal workload.
S0.quote: If they cut the teaching assistant's hours again, three kids in my class who need help with reading will just fall further behind.
fieldNote: She ties every worry to **named children**, not to herself.
Her pressure in this world is the **school budget**, which AI doesn't touch.
She's quiet in meetings but sees her role as feeding the **union rep** good facts.

steps.text: Keep teaching Year 4 and get faster at half-term data entry
Use the trust's planning tool for worksheets about once a week
Give the union rep reading data before the January budget meeting
Put £100 a month into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful for the boring parts, and I'd mean it. Writing forty end-of-year reports is where I'd want help first. I'd also say out loud that a laptop can't notice that Leo hasn't had breakfast, because someone has to keep saying that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the people above me will see AI marking and AI planning and decide one teacher can manage more kids, or that the teaching assistants can go. I'm junior, so if they don't replace people who leave, I'm the one doing two people's jobs. I don't think I'd lose my job, but I think it would get bigger and lonelier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the trust's AI training as soon as it's offered rather than wait, because once everyone uses it I'd rather know it well. I'd join the union's working group on AI and workload; Daniel keeps asking. And I'd keep three months saved, maybe push it to four, just in case they cut posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I think. I'm curious about it, but I can feel the squeeze coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at school would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Okafor, straight away. Teaching assistants do a lot of the reading groups and the photocopying and the data checking, and those are exactly the bits a tool could do on paper. On paper, I mean, because she also knows which kid is scared of the hand dryer, and no spreadsheet knows that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the job gets bigger, not gone. Is that a real comfort?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some comfort, yes. Parents still want a grown-up in the room with their eight-year-old, and that's not changing in a few years. If I'm honest though, a bigger job with less help is how people my age burn out and leave teaching after three years.

say: I'd say AI is welcome for **report writing** and other boring paperwork.
I'd keep saying out loud that software **can't notice** a hungry child.
think: I expect bosses to use AI to justify **bigger classes** or fewer assistants.
My job probably **gets bigger and lonelier**, which is how young teachers burn out.
do: Sign up for the trust's **AI training** as soon as it's offered.
Join the union's **working group** on AI and workload this year.
Grow savings from three to **four months** of bills in case posts get cut.
feel: **Curious** about the tools but **uneasy** about the squeeze behind them.
S1.quote: A bigger job with less help is how people my age burn out and leave teaching after three years.
fieldNote: She's open to the tools but reads them through **staffing cuts**.
Her loyalty to the **teaching assistant** shows how she sees the school as a team.
She doesn't fear losing her job, she fears **burning out** in it.

steps.text: Do the trust's AI report-writing training in the first term
Join the union's working group on AI and teacher workload
Build savings up to four months of bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in now, with rules for schools before tech companies sell them anything. I'd share the union's statement online, which I never do. At work I'd tell the kids it's fine, because they'd be scared too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a lot of what I do at a desk goes in 2028: planning, marking, the data, even explaining fractions, because a good AI tutor probably explains them better than I do now. What's left is the room: thirty-one kids, behaviour, safety, the hug after a bad day. I think the government would be tempted to say one teacher can supervise sixty with screens, and I'd be the cheap junior they keep or the extra one they drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd start a second qualification in special educational needs, because kids with high needs will always need people and the course is evening classes over two years. I'd stop the holiday we'd planned for next summer and save that £1,200. Once it arrives, I'd be at every union meeting, because if teachers don't push together it'll be decided for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. My stomach drops a bit. I'm twenty-seven and I chose this because it felt safe and useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kwame that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thank God one of us does a job a robot can't do until at least 2031. Even then, I don't see a robot putting in a drip on a frightened grandad. I'd ask him whether we should keep saving for a flat or wait to see what happens to my pay. He'd say keep saving; he always says keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the robots coming three years later, what does that change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weirdly, not much for me, because the hands-on bit of my job isn't lifting things, it's managing children. The three years matter more for Kwame and for Mrs Okafor, whose job is half hands-on. For me it's 2028 that counts, because that's when the planning and teaching part could go.

say: I'd demand **government rules** for AI in schools before companies sell anything.
I'd tell my class **it's fine** so the children don't get scared.
think: Planning, marking and even **explaining fractions** could go to AI by 2028.
I could become the **cheap junior** they keep, or the extra one they drop.
do: Start a two-year evening course in **special needs teaching** now.
Cancel next summer's holiday and save the **£1,200** instead.
Go to every **union meeting** once AGI arrives.
feel: **Anxious**, with a dropping stomach, because she chose teaching for **safety**.
S2.quote: Thank God one of us does a job a robot can't do until at least 2031.
fieldNote: She sees 2028 as the date that matters, because her work is **managing children**, not lifting.
She hedges by moving towards **special needs**, where people stay essential.
Her partner's **nursing job** is the household's anchor in this scenario.

steps.text: Enrol in a two-year evening course in special needs teaching
Cancel next summer's holiday and save the £1,200
Attend every union meeting about AI in schools
Share the union's call for government rules on school AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same as the fast one, but calmer. I'd say we have a few years, so let's use them, and schools should be planning now, not in 2030. I'd probably bring it up at a staff meeting, which is a big deal for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think five years is enough time for me to get properly good at this job and at something next to it. By 2031 I'd be in my seventh year, not my fourth, so I'd be less of a junior to cut. The planning and marking still go, but I'd have time to make myself the person who's good with the kids nobody else can reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the special needs course, but I'd start next September instead of rushing it in January. I'd keep saving the same hundred a month, and Kwame and I would keep going for a flat deposit, because by 2031 we want to own something. I'd also learn the AI tools properly, because if it's coming, I'd rather steer it than be steered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but a slower kind. It's the same cliff, just further away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in year three or four, while you can see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch which jobs at school go first. If they start using AI tutors for maths groups, I'd move myself towards the reading and the pastoral side, the kids who are struggling at home. And I'd ask the head about leading something, even something small like the reading scheme, because a job title helps when they decide who stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'steer it'. What does that look like for a second-year teacher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it looks like being the person in the room who has tried it and can say this bit helps, this bit is rubbish. Right now the older teachers ignore it and the head loves anything shiny. Someone needs to be in between, and that could be me.

say: I'd say we have **a few years**, so schools should plan now.
I'd raise it at a **staff meeting**, which is a big step for me.
think: By 2031 I'd be in my **seventh year** and harder to cut.
Planning and marking still go, so I'd aim at the **kids nobody reaches**.
do: Start the **special needs course** next September instead of rushing.
Keep saving **£100 a month** towards a flat deposit with my partner.
Ask the head to let me **lead the reading scheme**.
feel: **Anxious**, but a slower kind, like the **same cliff** further away.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time for me to get properly good at this job and at something next to it.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her from cornered to **planning ahead**.
She wants to be the **in-between teacher** who has actually tried the tools.
Owning a flat by 2031 is her **household goal** under every scenario.

steps.text: Start the special needs course next September
Test the school's AI tools and report what helps
Keep saving £100 a month towards a flat deposit
Aim to buy a flat with Kwame before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time if we use it, and I'd push for teachers to be trained properly over that decade instead of having stuff dumped on us. I'd be more hopeful in public in this one. Online I might even share some of the good things the tools do for kids with dyslexia.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is my whole early career. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, probably head of a year group or running special needs, and that kind of job is mostly people work. I'd still worry about the teaching assistants and about whether governments use it to cut, but for me, with ten years, I think I'd land on my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the special needs qualification at a normal pace, and use the tools every week until they're second nature. I'd stay active in the union and push for an agreement on AI and workload. Kwame and I would buy a flat in the next few years and probably start a family around 2030, same as we'd planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Not calm, but uneasy rather than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said governments might use it to cut. Who would you blame if they did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people setting budgets, not the technology. If a school gets a tool that does the data in five minutes, that time could go back to kids, or it could be used to sack someone. That's a choice, and it's a political one, which is why I'd vote for whoever promises to keep staff in classrooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, and that surprised me when I said it. If anything, knowing it's ten years away makes me want my kids to have a teacher who is a real person, so I'd fight for that. We'd still try around 2030.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty if teachers are trained properly.
I'd share how AI helps **children with dyslexia**.
think: By 2036 I'd likely run a **year group** or special needs, which is people work.
Cuts would be a **political choice** by budget-setters, not the technology's fault.
do: Finish the **special needs qualification** at a normal pace.
Push the union for a **workload agreement** on AI in schools.
Buy a flat in the next few years and **start a family** around 2030.
feel: **Uneasy rather than scared**, with real hope she'll land on her feet.
S4.quote: If a school gets a tool that does the data in five minutes, that time could go back to kids, or it could be used to sack someone.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her picture a **senior, people-heavy** role by 2036.
She blames **budget decisions**, not the tools, which fits her politics.
Her **family plans** stay the same, which she found surprising herself.

steps.text: Finish the special needs qualification over the next three years
Use the school's AI tools weekly until they're second nature
Vote for candidates who promise to keep staff in classrooms
Start trying for a baby with Kwame around 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, easily. Two years isn't enough to retrain, and I think the people making decisions would panic and cut, and juniors like me would be first. What would help is the government guaranteeing staff-to-child ratios in primary, so no one can replace a teacher with a screen and a teaching assistant, and paying for teachers like me to train in special needs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids. Everyone talks about what happens to teachers, but my class will be adults in the world you're describing, and I don't know what to teach them for. That's the thing that actually keeps me up a bit.

headlineQuote: My class will be adults in the world you're describing, and I don't know what to teach them for.
portrait: Bianca is a second-year **Year 4 teacher** at a city primary, living with her partner, a nurse.
She's careful with money, with about **three months** saved and a flat deposit as her goal.
She reads every AI change through **staffing cuts** and named children, and leans on the union.
Her fear peaks in the **2028 world**, and ten years lets her picture a senior people role.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because **two years** is too short to retrain and juniors would be cut first.
whatWouldHelp: Funded **special needs training** for junior teachers.
